unesco.title: Hayachine Kagura
unesco.description: In the fourteenth or fifteenth century, when the people of Iwate Prefecture in the northern part of mainland Japan worshipped Mt. Hayachine as a deity, they began a tradition of folk performance that continues to enliven the Great Festival of the Hayachine Shrine held in Hanamaki City on the first day of August. The Hayachine Kagura is a series of masked dances accompanied by drum, cymbals and flute: six ritual dances begin the performance; five dances recount stories of the deities and medieval Japanese history, and a final dance features a performer dressed as a ''shishi,'' an imaginary lion-like creature representing the Hayachine deity himself. Originally danced by holy officers of the Shrine to demonstrate the power of the mountain deity and bless the people, the Hayachine Kagura is now performed by representatives of the entire community, who take pride in their distinctive culture. To transmit and display the ritual is to reconfirm a sense of identity within the group and to contribute to the continuity of an important tradition. Its enactment also commemorates events from Japanese history and celebrates one of the mountain deities worshipped throughout the country.

profile.name: Hayachine Kagura
profile.tagline: A cycle of twelve masked ritual dances performed annually at Hayachine Shrine.
profile.insight: On August 1st, a performer dons a shishi mask to embody the mountain deity of Mount Hayachine, concluding a five-hour cycle of twelve ritual dances that have been performed since the 14th or 15th century.
profile.profile: Hayachine Kagura is a series of twelve masked ritual dances performed annually at the Hayachine Shrine in Hanamaki, Iwate, Japan. The cycle begins with six ritualistic dances, followed by five dances depicting medieval Japanese history and deities, and concludes with a performance by a shishi, a lion-like creature representing the mountain god. Originally performed by shrine officials, the tradition is now maintained by lay community members as a vital expression of local identity.
profile.profile_long:
The Hayachine Kagura is a ritual performance tradition centered at the Hayachine Shrine in Hanamaki, Iwate Prefecture, Japan. Dating back to the 14th or 15th century, the performance is deeply rooted in the worship of Mount Hayachine as a sacred deity. The tradition is believed to have been influenced by the practices of yamabushi, who were Buddhist ascetics living in the mountains. Scholars have also noted potential historical connections between the development of these dances and the evolution of Noh theater. In 2009, UNESCO recognized the cultural significance of this tradition by inscribing it on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

The performance structure consists of a sequence of twelve distinct dances, which together last approximately five hours. The cycle is divided into three thematic segments. The first six dances are strictly ritualistic in nature, including the Torimai (Bird Dance), the Okina (Old Man Dance), the Sanbasō (Third Old Man Dance), the Hachiman (War God Dance), the Yama no kami (Mountain God Dance), and the Iwato biraki (Opening of the Rock Cave). These are followed by five dances that recount stories from medieval Japanese history and the lives of various deities. The final dance features a performer wearing a shishi mask, representing an imaginary lion-like creature that serves as the personification of the mountain god of Hayachine.

Historically, the dances were performed exclusively by holy officers of the Shinto shrine as a means of purification and to demonstrate the power of the mountain deity while blessing the local people. Today, the role of the performer has shifted; the dances are now executed by representatives of the local community. This transition has turned the performance into a source of pride and a mechanism for maintaining group identity. While the full cycle is performed annually on August 1st at the Hayachine Shrine, shorter versions and 'discipleship' performances are held throughout the year in various locations across Iwate Prefecture and occasionally abroad.

The music accompanying the dancers is provided by a small ensemble using drums, cymbals, and flutes. The dancers themselves are masked, a defining visual element of the performance. Because the tradition is considered a sacred ritual, it is treated with specific protocols and respect, reflecting its origins as a Shinto ceremony. The continuity of the Hayachine Kagura is maintained through the active participation of lay practitioners who ensure the transmission of the ritual to future generations, keeping the connection to the mountain deity alive in the modern era.

sections.origins_and_history: The tradition dates to the 14th or 15th century, with historical influences attributed to the yamabushi, or mountain-dwelling Buddhist ascetics. Scholars have explored potential links between the development of the Kagura and the history of Noh theater.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The performance consists of twelve masked dances. The first six are ritualistic, followed by five historical or deity-focused dances, and a final dance featuring a shishi performer. The full cycle lasts approximately five hours.
sections.music_and_instruments: The dance is accompanied by an ensemble playing drums, cymbals, and flutes.
sections.costume_and_setting: Performers wear masks. The final dance features a performer dressed as a shishi, an imaginary lion-like creature.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The performance is held annually on August 1st at the Hayachine Shrine in Hanamaki to honor Seoritsu, the tutelary deity of Mount Hayachine.
sections.regional_variants: Discipleship performances are held throughout Iwate Prefecture, though these rarely feature the full twelve-dance cycle.
sections.lineage: A form of Kagura, influenced by yamabushi practices and potentially related to Noh theater.

profile.sacred_note: The Hayachine Kagura is a ritual dance performed in Shinto ceremonies in honor of the deity Seoritsu; it is a sacred tradition of the Hayachine Shrine.
